paper_title: SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates large language model inference by reducing the sequential cost of token-by-token generation. Advanced SD methods reduce proposal cost with parallel drafters that predict entire blocks in one forward pass, but overall speedup still depends on acceptance length. On-policy distillation (OPD) can push well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus, yet conventional pipelines collect supervision through sequential draft-and-verify rollouts. Our key insight is that on-policy supervision need not inherit these dependencies: a draft block can be supervised using only its reference prefix and draft-sampled history. We propose SpecOPD, a branch-parallel OPD framework that parallelizes draft sampling and target supervision across independent branches drawn from the evolving drafter policy at reference anchors. We pack these branches into proposal trees to share target-prefix computation, using tree masks for full attention, branch-consistent indexer groups for sparse attention, and indexed state replay for linear attention to preserve each branch's history. We train the drafter with an E2E-TV surrogate that directly targets acceptance length. Our study spans 8B full-attention (GQA), 27B full-linear (GQA--GDN), and 125B sparse-linear (QSA--GDN) targets, three parallel draft architectures (DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2), and four task domains (dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic). SpecOPD achieves up to 41.45% higher mean acceptance length, $16.09\times$ supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD under native configurations, and up to $3.56\times$ generation speedup over autoregressive decoding.

Introduction Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates autoregressive generation by verifying multiple tokens proposed by lightweight drafter in parallel [1, 2]. Parallel drafters such as DFlash reduce the cost of producing these SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding proposals by predicting an entire block in one forward pass [3, 23, 15, 25]. The overall speedup also depends on acceptance length, which draft training seeks to improve through better alignment with the target [29, 18]. To this end, common approach to draft training is supervised fine-tuning (SFT) [61] on fixed responses generated by the target model, following sequence-level knowledge distillation [62]. On-policy distillation (OPD) [28] has improved acceptance length beyond SFT plateaus by shifting training to blocks sampled from the current draft policy while retaining dense token-level target supervision [5]. However, in typical rollout-and-distill pipeline for SD-tailored OPD, collecting complete trajectories requires sequential draft-and-verify rounds [5]. The drafter proposes block, the target verifies it, and the accepted prefix determines where the next round begins. This dependency serializes response collection before drafter updates. The measured execution profile in the upper half of Figure 1a shows the alternation between rollout and training, with low GPU utilization during rollout collection. We therefore ask: Must on-policy training inherit the sequential dependencies of draft-and-verify rollouts? Luckily, these sequential dependencies are not inherent to on-policy supervision. We decouple on-policy supervision from full-response rollouts through unique twist to standard parallel drafter training [3, 23]: replacing reference-token labels with target supervision on draft-sampled prefixes. We sample anchors from pre-collected responses (regenerated offline by the target or supplied with the raw dataset) and use the current drafter to sample tokens for the masked positions. The target supervises each position using the reference prefix and preceding sampled tokens. Thanks to branch independence across anchors, draft sampling and target supervision can proceed in parallel without sequential full-trajectory collection during training. To put this parallelism to work, we propose SpecOPD, branch-parallel OPD framework for pushing well-trained drafters beyond acceptance-length plateaus without sequential full-response rollout collection. First, in proposal tree construction, the reference sequence forms shared reference trunk. We randomly sample anchors on this trunk, as in standard parallel-drafter training, and attach continuations sampled from the current drafter as draft branches. Second, in branch-parallel scoring, we reuse prefix computation while preserving each branchs history. For full attention (e.g., GQA [31]), we share trunk KV and use tree attention masks to restrict each branch to its reference prefix and own sampled history. For sparse attention (e.g., QSA [8]), branch-consistent compressed indexer groups preserve block selection after divergence. For linear attention (e.g., GDN [7]), masking alone cannot isolate recurrent states; we therefore use indexed state replay to restore anchor states from shared checkpoints and advance separate branch paths in parallel, avoiding repeated full-prefix execution. Finally, in acceptance-length optimization, we directly target acceptance length with the E2E-TV surrogate [6], which aggregates prefix products of drafttarget distribution overlap along each sampled branch. The measured execution profile in the lower half of Figure 1a shows the resulting higher GPU utilization. To summarize, our main contributions are: (1) Direct, parallel on-policy supervision. We observe that on-policy supervision for draft block requires only its reference context and draft-sampled history, without completing verified response. This yields direct on-policy alignment on draft-generated histories, independently across reference anchors. (2) Novel, efficient SD-tailored OPD. We propose SpecOPD to unify independent branch collection, shared-prefix target scoring, and E2E-TV acceptance-length optimization. Its executor preserves branch histories across full (GQA), sparse (QSA), and linear (GDN) attention layers, enabling parallel supervision with prefix reuse. (3) Broad, systematic empirical evaluation. We evaluate DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2 across 8B, 27B, and 125B targets with full, sparse, and linear attention on dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic tasks. SpecOPD improves mean AL by up to 41.45% and achieves 16.09 supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD (Figure 1b); measured generation speedup reaches 3.56 over AR. 2. Experiments We evaluate SpecOPDs inference efficiency, training efficiency, and the role of on-policy learning. (1) Inference efficiency. Our study spans 8B full-attention, 27B fulllinear, and 125B sparselinear targets; DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2; and dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic tasks at 𝑇 = 0 and 𝑇 = 1. These native-configuration measurements use the 27B target and eight high-performance GPUs and exclude offline reference preparation. (3) Gains from OPD. Setup Targets and Training. We study Qwen3-8B [66] with DFlash and DSpark, Qwen3.8-27B with DFlash V2, and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-125B with DFlash V2, covering full (GQA), fulllinear (GQAGDN), and sparselinear (QSAGDN) attention. We evaluate decoding on MT-Bench [10], HumanEval [11], MATH-500 [12], and recorded SWE [13] and Terminal [14] interaction histories. The latter measure continuation efficiency from recorded contexts; Appendix A.1 describes the collections. Acceptance comparisons use each drafters original checkpoint; training comparisons use sequential-rollout OPD, off-policy CE, and off-policy E2E-TV. This improvement combines 4.95 faster updates with 3.25 more supervised tokens per update: branch parallelism both reduces collection time and supplies more supervised positions at each step. Draft-OPD alternates dependent rollout, replay/training, and weight-update stages; SpecOPD batches drafting and target scoring across reference anchors. Mean recorded GPU activity rises from 26.37% to 77.23% in the illustrated windows. The profile illustrates how branch parallelism keeps the GPUs active during training. Appendix B.2 specifies the timing and profiling procedures. 3.4. Ablation Study On-Policy vs. Off-Policy. We compare SpecOPD with two off-policy baselines trained on fixed targetgenerated responses: CE uses reference-token labels, while E2E-TV matches target distributions along reference histories. At matched optimizer steps and reference-sequence batches, the SpecOPD recipe achieves higher acceptance on all three benchmarks, with mean advantage of up to 15.71% over offpolicy E2E-TV (Figure 8). SpecOPD also improves on the common initialization, whereas the evaluated off-policy checkpoints fall below it. The recipes use different compute allocations and gradient paths; Appendix A.6 gives the configurations and complete comparison. Training Dynamics. Lower training loss does not necessarily translate into longer acceptance. All three runs reduce training loss, but off-policy CEs acceptance declines as training continues, while SpecOPDs improves (Figure 8ad). These trends motivate evaluating acceptance directly alongside the training objective. Where Acceptance Changes. closer look at prefix survival shows how the gains are distributed across draft positions (Figure 8e), relative to the common initialization. Using each methods best evaluated checkpoint by mean AL, SpecOPD improves survival across all seven positions, whereas both off-policy baselines show declines. At position seven, survival rises by 4.33 percentage points, compared with 2.57-point decline for off-policy CE. These request-level measurements connect the training comparison to the accepted-prefix behavior that determines decoding progress. Related Work Parallel Drafting for SD. Speculative decoding (SD) accelerates generation by verifying inexpensive draft proposals with the target in parallel [1, 2]. Auxiliary-head and self-speculative approaches improve proposal efficiency through multiple prediction heads or target-layer reuse [27, 36, 53, 54]. Tree-based verification and confidence-aware candidate allocation improve coverage and budget utilization [26, 17, 32, 35], while retrievalbased and hybrid approaches exploit datastores, cached token transitions, or target logits to provide inexpensive candidates [33, 34, 37, 38]. Many drafters reuse target representations: EAGLE drafts autoregressively from target features [16, 17, 18], and multi-token prediction (MTP) heads trained with the target serve as built-in drafters [19, 20]. Autoregressive drafting still spends one drafter pass per proposed token; parallel drafters instead predict block in one forward pass. Falcon drafts semi-autoregressively [21], PARD adapts small draft model to parallel mask prediction [22], and P-EAGLE turns EAGLE into parallel multi-token predictor [23]. DFlash brings block diffusion to drafting [3]. DFlare enlarges draft capacity with per-layer target-feature fusion [24]. Domino decouples parallel drafting from causal modeling, using lightweight causal head to refine parallel draft outputs [25]; DSpark combines parallel backbone with lightweight sequential modeling and confidence-scheduled verification [15]. D-cut further adapts verification depth across batched requests to balance acceptance and verification cost [47]. These designs improve how proposals are generated and verified. SpecOPD addresses their training: fresh supervision for parallel drafters can be collected across independent reference anchors, without constructing complete verified trajectory at every collection step. Appendix expands these directions and discusses their connections to RL rollouts and multimodal generation. On-Policy Draft Training and Acceptance Objectives. On-policy distillation supervises student-generated histories [28]. DistillSpec studies draft-generated data and decoding-aware divergence choices [29]; DraftOPD uses target-assisted rollouts and error-state replay [5]. Acceptance objectives account for progress beyond tokenwise accuracy: E2E-TV couples distribution overlap across draft prefixes [6], while Expected Decoding Rounds models verification-round progress [30]. SpecOPD adopts E2E-TV and parallelizes fresh sampling and history-consistent target scoring, complementing efforts to reduce training memory [55] and communication [56]. Its supervision is on-policy within each branch; reference prefixes define the outer contexts and differ from unrestricted full-response rollouts. Shared Computation across Histories. Tree attention, introduced by SpecInfer [26] and adopted by Medusa [27], makes multiple candidate paths jointly verifiable while preserving their ancestry. Reusing computation for training must also accommodate targets with different history representations: GQA retains token KV [31], QSA selects token blocks using compressed indexer keys [8], and GDN maintains recurrent state [7]. SpecOPD uses common proposal tree to organize this reuse, with tree masks, branch-consistent indexer groups, and indexed state replay for the respective attention types. Their common principle is prefix reuse with separate histories after divergence. 5. Conclusion SpecOPD unlocks faster lossless decoding through elegant, efficient branch-parallel on-policy learning built on simple insight: draft block can learn directly from target supervision on its own sampled histories. unique twist on parallel-drafter training replaces reference-token labels with target supervision on draftsampled histories, while proposal trees enable parallel scoring with shared-prefix reuse. Our study spans 8B full attention (GQA), 27B fulllinear (GQAGDN), and 125B sparselinear (QSAGDN) targets, using DFlash, DSpark, and DFlash V2 across dialogue, coding, mathematics, and agentic tasks. SpecOPD improves mean acceptance length by up to 41.45% and achieves 16.09 supervised-token throughput over sequential-rollout OPD; measured generation speedup reaches 3.56 over autoregressive decoding. This framework enables the community to explore better policies across heterogeneous targets and translate advances in draft learning into faster production serving.

Auxiliary heads, target features, multi-token prediction, and self-speculation improve proposal generation [27, 16, 18, 19, 20, 36]. SWIFT adapts layer skipping online without training [53]; KNN-SSD retrieves input-dependent layer sets [54]. Candidate trees support joint verification [26, 17], while TALON and ECHO allocate candidates using confidence [35, 32]. D-cut jointly prunes draft depth across batched requests using confidence and verification cost [47]. Retrieval supplies candidates from datastores, cached transitions, or target logits [33, 34, 37]; GRAFT combines retrieval and pruning [38]. Other systems overlap drafting and verification or use rollback-aware branches [39, 40, 41]. Parallel and semi-autoregressive architectures reduce serial proposal cost [21, 22, 23, 24, 25], including block diffusion in DFlash and lightweight sequential modeling over parallel backbone in DSpark [3, 15]. These inference mechanisms can accompany drafter learning when proposal distributions and verification rules are preserved. On-Policy Draft Training and Acceptance Objectives. Fixed reference responses differ from drafter-generated histories. Generalized on-policy distillation supervises student-induced contexts [28]; DistillSpec studies draftgenerated data and decoding-aware divergences [29]; Draft-OPD uses target-assisted rollouts and error-state replay [5]. EAGLE-3 also accounts for generated draft inputs during training [18]. Because acceptance stops at the first rejection, tokenwise accuracy alone does not determine progress. BeBops E2E-TV couples distribution overlap across prefixes [6], while Expected Decoding Rounds models progress across verification rounds [30]. SpecOPD supplies fresh branch samples and history-consistent target distributions to E2E-TV through parallel collection and scoring, complementing efforts to reduce training memory [55] and communication [56]. Its supervision is on-policy within each branch; reference prefixes remain distinct from unrestricted rollout contexts. Collection policy, scoring, and objective choice are separate experimental factors. Shared Computation across Histories. SpecInfer and Medusa jointly score candidate paths through tree attention [26, 27]. Shared ancestors permit reuse, but divergent tokens require separate histories. KVShot studies complementary representation issue: target KV preserves context that hidden states may discard, while introducing query-estimation and gradient-sparsity challenges [48]. History preservation also depends on the target architecture: GQA stores token KV [31], QSA selects blocks through compressed indexer keys [8], and GDN maintains recurrent state [7]. Branch-parallel supervision therefore combines tree masks, branchconsistent indexer groups, and indexed state restoration and replay. Training additionally requires numerically consistent supervision at every sampled position, beyond identifying an accepted inference prefix. At the model level, HMI shares hierarchical components across tenants [57], while FloE reduces expert-loading costs through compression and sparse prediction [58]; these mechanisms address model memory and movement rather than branch-history consistency. 26 SpecOPD: Branch-Parallel On-Policy Distillation for Speculative Decoding Speculative Decoding for RL Rollouts. RL post-training couples repeated trajectory generation with an evolving policy. SPEC-RL reuses earlier trajectory segments [42]; SRT refreshes per-prompt continuation trees [43]. Integrated systems support synchronous and asynchronous speculative rollouts [44], and BeBop combines MTP with rejection sampling [6]. TailSieve isolates long-tail requests and allocates route-specialized replicas using MTP or DFlash [49]. Branch-parallel supervision could help refresh learned drafters as the policy changes; this would require version-consistent target supervision and update costs amortized by rollout savings. Multimodal Speculative Decoding. Visual inputs introduce distinct encoding, prefilling, and decoding bottlenecks [59]. SpecVLM prunes draft-side video tokens while retaining full-target verification [45]; ParallelVLM combines visual-alignment-aware pruning with parallel draftverify execution [46]. LVSpec instead relaxes verification away from visual anchors, changing the criterion rather than preserving exact targetdistribution equivalence [50]. Complementary methods reduce conditioning costs through token selection in OmniDelta [51] or head-specific cache compression for multimodal LMs in HybridKV and AR video diffusion in Forcing-KV [60, 52]. Shared visual prefixes could support branch-parallel drafter training, but this extension remains unevaluated. It would require consistent visual features, positions, and cache semantics across branches; exactness relative to an uncompressed target would also require preserving its verification distribution.
